items.prompt:
Read the class discussion below:
  Teacher: 'What makes a good friend?'
  Ava: 'A good friend is kind and helps you.'
  Ben: 'I agree with Ava. A good friend is also honest — they tell you the truth even when it is hard.'
  Cara: 'I want to talk about dogs.'
Which student does NOT follow the discussion rules, and why?
A) Ava — she only gave one idea
B) Ben — he agreed instead of disagreeing
C) Cara — she changed the topic, which breaks the rule about staying on the topic under discussion
items.answer: C) Cara — she changed the topic, which breaks the rule about staying on the topic under discussion

steps: Ava gives a relevant answer — fine.
Ben agrees and adds new information — good discussion behavior.
Cara introduces a completely different topic (dogs) during a discussion about friendship.
Discussion rules require students to speak about the topics under discussion.

items.prompt:
A student wants to disagree with a classmate respectfully. Which response is best?
A) 'That is a terrible idea.'
B) 'I see it differently — I think the character was scared, not brave, because she was shaking.'
C) 'You're wrong and I'll tell everyone why.'
items.answer: B) 'I see it differently — I think the character was scared, not brave, because she was shaking.'

steps: Option A is disrespectful — it dismisses the idea without explanation.
Option C is confrontational and not respectful.
Option B disagrees but explains WHY, using evidence from the text ('she was shaking').
Respectful disagreement means stating your view and backing it up, not attacking the speaker.

items.prompt:
A student says something confusing during discussion. Two classmates have different reactions:
  Student A ignores it and waits for the teacher to move on.
  Student B asks: 'I'm not sure I understand what you mean. Can you give an example?'
Whose response better follows discussion rules?
A) Student A
B) Student B
C) Both are equally good

steps: When something is confusing, the discussion rule is to ask for clarification and further explanation.
Student B asks a clarifying question — 'Can you give an example?' — to deepen understanding.
Student A ignores the confusion and misses an opportunity to clarify.
Asking good clarifying questions helps the whole group understand better.

items.prompt:
Read these student responses to the question 'Why do you think the main character decided to share her lunch?':
  Response 1: 'Because she is nice.'
  Response 2: 'She is nice, just like Jonah said, and the story says she remembered when someone shared with her — so she was paying it forward.'
Which response better demonstrates building on others' talk with a text connection?
A) Response 1
B) Response 2
C) Both are equally strong

steps: Response 1 gives an answer but does not link to a classmate or use text evidence.
Response 2 (a) links to a classmate's comment ('just like Jonah said') and (b) uses text evidence ('the story says she remembered').
Response 2 demonstrates both building on others' talk AND supporting with evidence.

items.prompt:
A teacher notices that three students do all the talking and five students never speak. What discussion rule is the group NOT following?
A) Speaking one at a time
B) Making sure everyone has a chance to participate — balanced, collaborative conversation
C) Staying on topic
items.answer: B) Making sure everyone has a chance to participate — balanced, collaborative conversation

steps: Collaborative discussions involve everyone, not just a few voices.
When five students never speak, the conversation is not truly collaborative.
Part of following discussion rules is ensuring fair participation — not dominating or being left out.

items.prompt:
A student starts every response with: 'I was going to say...' but then says the same idea the previous speaker already shared. What mistake is she making?
A) Using complete sentences
B) Not listening carefully enough to notice her idea was already stated
C) Asking too many questions
items.answer: B) Not listening carefully enough to notice her idea was already stated

steps: If a student repeats what was just said, it usually means she was not listening carefully.
Good collaborative conversation requires listening to others so you can BUILD on or ADJUST your contribution.
Careful listening is one of the core discussion rules.

items.prompt:
Read this exchange:
  Diego: 'I think the wolf in the story is misunderstood.'
  Fatima: 'What do you mean by misunderstood?'
  Diego: 'I mean everyone thinks he is bad, but maybe he was just trying to survive.'
What is Fatima doing, and why is it helpful?
A) Fatima is interrupting, which is against the rules
B) Fatima is asking for clarification and further explanation, which helps everyone understand Diego's thinking
C) Fatima is changing the subject
items.answer: B) Fatima is asking for clarification and further explanation, which helps everyone understand Diego's thinking

steps: Fatima asks 'What do you mean by misunderstood?' — this is a direct request for clarification.
Her question allows Diego to explain his thinking more fully.
This benefits the whole group — now everyone understands what Diego meant.
Asking for clarification is explicitly part of the 2.SL.A.1 standard.

items.prompt:
A student says: 'I want to add onto what Maya said about birds migrating. I think that connects to what we learned about butterflies — they migrate too.' What skills is this student demonstrating?
A) Only topic knowledge
B) Building on others' talk by linking remarks across the discussion
C) Gaining the floor disrespectfully
items.answer: B) Building on others' talk by linking remarks across the discussion

steps: 'I want to add onto what Maya said' shows the student is linking their comment to a classmate's remark.
By connecting the butterfly information to Maya's bird comment, the student builds a broader discussion.
This demonstrates the skill of building on others' talk and connecting ideas.

items.prompt:
During a small group discussion, one student keeps giving very long answers that use up all the time. What should the group do?
A) Let her keep talking since she knows the most
B) Politely ask her to pause so others can share: 'That is great — can we hear from someone else too?'
C) Stop having discussions
items.answer: B) Politely ask her to pause so others can share: 'That is great — can we hear from someone else too?'

steps: Collaborative discussions require balanced participation.
Politely inviting others to share ('can we hear from someone else?') is a respectful way to ensure everyone participates.
This follows the spirit of collaborative discussion rules without being rude.

items.prompt:
A student says: 'I'm not sure I understand — did you mean that the character was afraid of the dark, or afraid of being alone?' What kind of question is this?
A) A question that changes the topic
B) A clarifying question that checks whether the student understood correctly
C) A rude interruption
items.answer: B) A clarifying question that checks whether the student understood correctly

steps: This question stays on the same topic and offers two possible interpretations.
It asks the speaker to confirm which one they meant — this is seeking clarification.
Clarifying questions help everyone in the discussion understand the speaker's meaning more precisely.

items.prompt:
In a class discussion about weather, one student says: 'It rains because clouds get too heavy with water.' Another student says: 'Building on that, the water then falls because gravity pulls it down.' Which discussion skill does the second student show?
A) Changing the topic
B) Linking their comment to a classmate's remark to add new information
C) Repeating what the first student said
items.answer: B) Linking their comment to a classmate's remark to add new information

steps: 'Building on that' is explicit link language — the student signals they are connecting to the previous comment.
The student adds new related information (gravity), not just repeating what was said.
This demonstrates building on others' talk: linking and extending.

items.prompt:
A discussion about community helpers is getting off track — students are now talking about their favorite TV shows. Whose job is it to steer the discussion back on topic?
A) Only the teacher
B) Only the student who changed the subject
C) Everyone — students can also ask 'Can we get back to community helpers?' to help refocus
items.answer: C) Everyone — students can also ask 'Can we get back to community helpers?' to help refocus

steps: In collaborative discussions, all participants share responsibility for keeping the conversation on topic.
Any student can politely ask to refocus: 'Can we get back to...?'
This is a sign of strong discussion participation and leadership.

items.prompt:
A student listens to a classmate's idea about a book and then says: 'I heard you say the ending was confusing. I felt that way too, but I think it was confusing ON PURPOSE — to make us think.' Which skills does this response show?
A) Restating what was heard AND adding a new interpretation
B) Ignoring what the classmate said
C) Asking an off-topic question
items.answer: A) Restating what was heard AND adding a new interpretation

steps: 'I heard you say the ending was confusing' shows the student listened and recapped what they heard.
'I felt that way too, but...' shows agreement followed by a new connected interpretation.
Restating + building is a high-quality collaborative discussion move.

items.prompt:
Why is it important to follow agreed-upon rules during a classroom discussion?
A) Because the teacher will give you a bad grade if you don't
B) Because rules ensure everyone is heard, respected, and the conversation stays productive
C) Because rules mean only smart students can speak
items.answer: B) Because rules ensure everyone is heard, respected, and the conversation stays productive

steps: Discussion rules are not about grades — they are about making the conversation fair and useful.
Rules like listening, taking turns, and staying on topic ensure every voice is heard.
When rules are followed, discussions are more productive and everyone learns more.

items.prompt:
A student says: 'I want to add to what Priya said, but I also want to ask her something. Priya, you said flowers need sunlight — but what about plants that grow underground, like carrots?' What two discussion skills is this student using?
A) Building on Priya's comment AND asking a clarifying question
B) Changing the topic AND interrupting
C) Repeating Priya's idea AND asking an off-topic question
items.answer: A) Building on Priya's comment AND asking a clarifying question

steps: 'I want to add to what Priya said' = building on others' talk.
'What about plants that grow underground?' = asking a clarifying question that extends the discussion.
This response demonstrates two strong discussion skills simultaneously.
